source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Reveal Interpretable and Steerable Features in VLA Models
source.authors: Aiden Swann; Lachlain McGranahan; Hugo Buurmeijer; Monroe Kennedy; Mac Schwager

page_placements.theme: Many units in other domains and architectures lack a single-concept description

record.tranche_reason: Uses sparse autoencoders as a tool for finding and steering VLA features, but does not test the listed claims about polysemantic neurons or their causes.
record.gate_note: The paper measures how often sampled SAE features and FFN neurons meet its human interpretability criterion. That is not a direct measure of polysemanticity: it does not test whether a neuron responds to several unrelated inputs, or whether those inputs share a feature the model uses. Only the FFN-neuron measurement is recorded as a related finding; cited results from other work are excluded.
record.test_reason: The study trains SAEs on VLA residual streams and reports interpretability, generality and steering of SAE features. Its only neuron-level result is that 6/20 sampled FFN neurons in π0.5 DROID PG5 were judged interpretable. That is a human interpretability judgment. It does not measure whether neurons respond to several unrelated inputs, and it tests no cause, architecture effect or measurement dependence. A VLA model is also not the image classifier of V1 or the language model of V2.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors say SAEs give a substantially more interpretable basis for temporal VLA behavior than raw FFN neurons (79.2% vs 30% of sampled units). They add that FFN neurons can still contain meaningful steerable directions.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains TopK SAEs with AuxK on VLA residual-stream activations and evaluates temporal feature interpretability and steering; it does not reproduce the cited original methods for neuron polysemanticity.

fits_no_version.finding: In π0.5-DROID PaliGemma layer 5, 6 of 20 randomly sampled FFN neurons were labeled interpretable under a temporal event/state criterion. Of the layer's 16,384 FFN neurons, 281 never fired on the DROID subset.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a VLA model, most sampled raw FFN neurons do not align with a single identifiable sensorimotor event or state under human labeling.

record.problems: The FFN-neuron result is based on a sample of 20 and a human interpretability judgment, not a direct polysemanticity measure. The paper also notes limited robotics data and that per-token SAE features are generally less interpretable.
record.rows_left_out: SAE feature interpretability sampling results (95/120 overall and the per-dictionary counts in Table 8) are omitted because they measure SAE features rather than the claim's individual neurons. Other steering and ablation results concern SAE features and robot behavior, not neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No count of language-model MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts. The VLA FFN neurons get only an interpretability rate.
The superposition cause is assumed in the SAE motivation, not tested.
No test of initialization, regularization or training noise as causes.
No comparison across activation functions, architectures or regularization of neuron polysemanticity.
No reanalysis of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No comparison across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's own SAE-versus-neuron comparison uses a sample of only 20 neurons from one layer. The related work asserts that FFN features are 'highly superposed', but the paper assumes this rather than tests it. The SAE feature results are correctly left out of the rows.

versions.untested_parts: No image-classifier neuron test or measurement of responses to unrelated image inputs.
No language-model MLP neuron analysis of responses to unrelated tokens or contexts.
The paper uses SAEs to extract features but does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by capacity pressure or superposition.
No test of initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
No comparison of polysemanticity across activation functions, architectures, or regularization settings.
The study does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons or test whether apparently unrelated activations share a feature.
No comparison of polysemanticity measurements across activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: π0.5
rows.operation_detail: Sampled FFN neurons were assessed with the study's temporal activation and feature-search pipeline, then manually labeled for interpretability.

conditions.value: temporal activation pattern aligns with an identifiable event or state

rows.note: This is an interpretability judgment, not a test of whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs. The paper also states that 16,103 of 16,384 FFN neurons fired at least once in the DROID subset.
rows.check: The row's subject and value are read correctly (6/20, Table 8, Appendix D.1). The row is a comparator: the authors' own SAE method is set against an adapted FFN-neuron baseline. 'Non-interpretable' is not the same as polysemantic, so no version's effect can be read from it. The 'interpretable' criterion is temporal alignment with an identifiable event or state.

relation.reason: It uses the premise that FFN features are superposed to motivate SAEs. The neuron comparisons (interpretability, steering) are comparators and do not test polysemanticity.

tranche.reason: The study trains SAEs on VLA activations, motivated by superposed FFN features. Its FFN-neuron result is a baseline for its own method, measuring human-judged temporal interpretability, not whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs.

source_check.notes: The FFN baseline adapts Häon et al. and labels only 20 neurons from one layer (π0.5 DROID PG5). Non-interpretable is not the same as polysemantic. FFN-neuron steering baselines (Tables 3-4) are also comparators, not polysemanticity measures. No verdicts are warranted.

statements.problem: none. 6/20, 16,384 and 281 inactive all match Appendix D.1 and Table 8. The text itself says PG5 is PaliGemma layer 5 (Fig. 1 caption, Sec. 5.4). Random sampling follows from the 'same 20-feature sampling' protocol.
